The Far 3 kiloparsecs Arm was discovered in 2008 by astronomer Tom Dame (Center for Astrophysics | Harvard & Smithsonian). It is located in the first galactic quadrant at a distance of 3 kiloparsecs (about 10,000 light years) from the Galactic Center.
A simulation published in 2011 suggested that the Milky Way may have obtained its spiral arm structure as a result of repeated collisions with the Sagittarius Dwarf Elliptical Galaxy.

It has been suggested that the Milky Way contains two different spiral patterns: an inner one, formed by the Sagittarius arm, that rotates fast, and an outer one, formed by the Carina and Perseus arms, whose rotation velocity is slower and whose arms are tightly wound. In this scenario, suggested by numerical simulations of the dynamics of the different spiral arms, the outer pattern would form an outer pseudoring, and the two patterns would be connected by the Cygnus arm.

Outside of the major spiral arms is the Monoceros Ring (or Outer Ring), a ring of gas and stars torn from other galaxies billions of years ago. However, several members of the scientific community recently restated their position, affirming the Monoceros structure is nothing more than an over-density produced by the flared and warped thick disk of the Milky Way. The structure of the Milky Way's disk is warped along an "S" curve.
## Halo

The galactic disk is surrounded by a spheroidal halo of old stars and globular clusters and contains most of the Milky Way's dark matter. It is moderately triaxial in shape, with the longest axis tilted about 25 degrees above the disk and 24 degrees ahead of the Sun. Its density seems to obey a power law with two breaks at around 15 and 30 kiloparsecs (49 and 98 kly). However, a few globular clusters have been found farther, such as PAL 4 and AM 1 at more than 200,000 light-years from the Galactic Center. About 40 percent of the Milky Way's clusters are on retrograde orbits, which means they move in the opposite direction from the Milky Way rotation. The globular clusters can follow rosette orbits about the Milky Way, in contrast to the elliptical orbit of a planet around a star.

Although the disk contains dust that obscures the view at some wavelengths, the halo component does not. Active star formation takes place in the disk (especially in the spiral arms, which represent areas of high density), but does not take place in the halo, as there is little cool gas to collapse into stars. Open clusters are also located primarily on the disk.

Discoveries in the early 21st century have added new dimensions to our understanding of the Milky Way's structure. With the discovery that the disk of the Andromeda Galaxy (M31) extends much farther than previously thought, the possibility of the disk of the Milky Way extending farther is apparent, and this is supported by evidence from the discovery of the Outer Arm extension of the Cygnus Arm and of a similar extension of the Scutum–Centaurus Arm. With the discovery of the Sagittarius Dwarf Elliptical Galaxy came the discovery of a ribbon of galactic debris as the polar orbit of the dwarf and its interaction with the Milky Way tears it apart. Upon the 2004 discovery of a ring of galactic debris in an in-plane orbit around the Milky Way, it was initially believed that the debris was the remnant of a system dubbed the Canis Major Dwarf Galaxy. Other scholars believed it to be due to the Galactic warp, a view which has been supported by more recent evidence as of 2021.

The Sloan Digital Sky Survey of the northern sky shows a huge, diffuse structure (spread across an area about 5,000 times the size of a full moon) within the Milky Way that does not seem to fit current models. The collection of stars rises nearly perpendicular to the plane of the Milky Way's spiral arms. The proposed likely interpretation is that a dwarf galaxy is merging with the Milky Way. This galaxy is tentatively named the Virgo Stellar Stream and is found in the direction of Virgo about 30,000 light-years (9 kiloparsecs) away.
## Gaseous halo

In addition to the stellar halo, the Chandra X-ray Observatory, XMM-Newton, and Suzaku have provided evidence that there is also a gaseous halo containing a large amount of hot gas. This halo extends for hundreds of thousands of light-years, much farther than the stellar halo and close to the distance of the Large and Small Magellanic Clouds. The mass of this hot halo is nearly equivalent to the mass of the Milky Way itself. The temperature of this halo gas is between 1 and 2. 5 million K (1. 8 and 4. 5 million degrees Fahrenheit).

Observations of distant galaxies indicate that the universe had about one-sixth as much baryonic (ordinary) matter as dark matter when it was just a few billion years old. However, only about half of those baryons are accounted for in the modern universe based on observations of nearby galaxies like the Milky Way. If the finding that the mass of the halo is comparable to the mass of the Milky Way is confirmed, it could be the identity of the missing baryons around the Milky Way.
## Contents

The Milky Way contains between 100 and 400 billion stars and at least that many planets. An exact figure would depend on counting the number of very-low-mass stars, which are difficult to detect, especially at distances of more than 300 light years (90 parsecs) from the Sun. As a comparison, the neighboring Andromeda Galaxy contains an estimated one trillion (1012) stars. The Milky Way may contain ten billion white dwarfs, a billion neutron stars, and a hundred million stellar black holes. Filling the space between the stars is a disk of gas and dust called the interstellar medium. This disk has at least a comparable extent in radius to the stars, whereas the thickness of the gas layer ranges from hundreds of light-years for the colder gas to thousands of light-years for the warmer gas.

The disk of stars in the Milky Way does not have a sharp edge beyond which there are no stars. Rather, the concentration of stars decreases with distance from the center of the Milky Way. Beyond a radius of roughly 40,000 light-years (13 kiloparsecs) from the center, the number of stars per cubic parsec drops much faster with radius. Surrounding the galactic disk is a spherical galactic halo of stars and globular clusters that extends farther outward, but is limited in size by the orbits of two Milky Way satellites, the Large and Small Magellanic Clouds, whose closest approach to the Galactic Center is about 180,000 light years (55 kiloparsecs). At this distance or beyond, the orbits of most halo objects would be disrupted by the Magellanic Clouds. Hence, such objects would probably be ejected from the vicinity of the Milky Way. The integrated absolute visual magnitude of the Milky Way is estimated to be around minus 20. 9.

Both gravitational microlensing and planetary transit observations indicate that there may be at least as many planets bound to stars as there are stars in the Milky Way, and microlensing measurements indicate that there are more rogue planets not bound to host stars than there are stars. The Milky Way contains an average of at least one planet per star, resulting in 100–400 billion planets, according to a January 2013 study of the five-planet star system Kepler-32 by the Kepler space observatory. A different January 2013 analysis of Kepler data estimated that at least 17 billion Earth-sized exoplanets reside in the Milky Way.

In November 2013, astronomers reported, based on Kepler space telescope data, that there could be as many as 40 billion Earth-sized planets orbiting in the habitable zones of Sun-like stars and red dwarfs within the Milky Way. 11 billion of these estimated planets may be orbiting Sun-like stars. The nearest exoplanet may be 4. 2 light-years away, orbiting the red dwarf Proxima Centauri, according to a 2016 study. Such Earth-sized planets may be more numerous than gas giants, though harder to detect at great distances given their small size. Besides exoplanets, "exocomets", comets beyond the Solar System, have also been detected and may be common in the Milky Way. More recently, in November 2020, over 300 million habitable exoplanets are estimated to exist in the Milky Way Galaxy.
When compared to other more distant galaxies in the universe, the Milky Way galaxy has a below average amount of neutrino luminosity making our galaxy a "neutrino desert".
## Formation

The oldest stars in the Milky Way probably formed shortly after the Dark Ages of the early universe. The oldest stars are spherically distributed in the galaxy, suggesting it started out in a spherical shape. As the mass of the early galaxy condensed any small rotation about the center was amplified by conservation of angular momentum, causing the spherical shape to flatten into a spiral disk. Later generations of stars formed in this spiral disk. Most younger stars, including the Sun, are observed to be in the disk.

Assuming the Milky Way is similar to other galaxies, 40 percent of its mass may have come from other galaxies. Since the first stars began to form, the Milky Way has grown through both galaxy mergers (particularly early in the Milky Way's growth) and accretion of gas directly from the Galactic halo. The Milky Way is currently accreting material from several small galaxies, including two of its largest satellite galaxies, the Large and Small Magellanic Clouds, through the Magellanic Stream. Direct accretion of gas is observed in high-velocity clouds like the Smith Cloud.

Cosmological simulations indicate that, 11 billion years ago, it merged with a particularly large galaxy that has been labeled the Kraken. Properties of the Milky Way such as stellar mass, angular momentum, and metallicity in its outermost regions suggest it has undergone no mergers with large galaxies in the last 10 billion years. This lack of recent major mergers is unusual among spiral galaxies of a similar type. Its neighbor, the Andromeda Galaxy, appears to have a more typical history, shaped by more recent mergers with relatively large galaxies.

According to recent studies, the Milky Way as well as the Andromeda Galaxy lie in what in the galaxy color–magnitude diagram is known as the "green valley", a region populated by galaxies in transition from the "blue cloud" (galaxies actively forming new stars) to the "red sequence" (galaxies that lack star formation). Star-formation activity in green valley galaxies is slowing as they run out of star-forming gas in the interstellar medium. In simulated galaxies with similar properties, star formation will typically have been extinguished within about five billion years from now, even accounting for the expected, short-term increase in the rate of star formation due to the collision between both the Milky Way and the Andromeda Galaxy. Measurements of other galaxies similar to the Milky Way suggest it is among the reddest and brightest spiral galaxies that are still forming new stars and it is just slightly bluer than the bluest red sequence galaxies.
## Age and cosmological history

Globular clusters are among the oldest objects in the Milky Way, thereby setting a lower limit on the age of the Milky Way. The ages of individual stars in the Milky Way can be estimated by measuring the abundance of long-lived radioactive elements such as thorium-232 and uranium-238, then comparing the results to estimates of their original abundance, a technique called nucleocosmochronology. These yield values of about 12. 5 plus or minus 3 billion years for CS 31082-001 and 13. 8 plus or minus 4 billion years for BD +17 degrees 3248.

Once a white dwarf forms, it begins to cool radiatively, and its surface temperature steadily drops. By measuring the temperatures of the coolest of these white dwarfs and comparing them to their expected initial temperatures, an age estimate can be made. With this technique, the age of the globular cluster M4 was estimated as 12. 7 plus or minus 0. 7 billion years. Age estimates for the oldest of these clusters yield a best-fit age of 12. 6 billion years and a 95 percent confidence upper limit of 16 billion years.

In November 2018, astronomers reported the discovery of one of the universe's oldest stars. About 13. 5 billion years old, 2MASS J18082002-5104378 B is a tiny ultra metal-poor (UMP) star made almost entirely of materials released from the Big Bang, and is possibly one of the first stars. The discovery of the star in the Milky Way Galaxy suggests that the galaxy may be at least 3 billion years older than previously thought.

Several individual stars have been found in the Milky Way's halo with measured ages very close to the 13. 80-billion-year age of the universe. In 2007, a star in the galactic halo, HE 1523-0901, was estimated to be about 13. 2 billion years old. As the oldest known object in the Milky Way at that time, this measurement placed a lower limit on the age of the Milky Way. This estimate was made using the UV-Visual Echelle Spectrograph of the Very Large Telescope to measure the relative strengths of spectral lines caused by the presence of thorium and other elements created by the R-process. The line strengths yield abundances of different elemental isotopes, from which an estimate of the age of the star can be derived using nucleocosmochronology. Another star, HD 140283, has been estimated at either 13. 7 plus or minus 0. 7 billion years, 12. 2 plus or minus 0. 6 billion years, or 12. 0 plus or minus 0. 5 billion years.
According to observations using adaptive optics to correct for Earth's atmospheric distortion, stars in the galaxy's bulge are about 12. 8 billion years old.

The age of stars in the galactic thin disk has also been estimated using nucleocosmochronology. Measurements of thin disk stars yield an estimate that the thin disk formed 8. 8 plus or minus 1. 7 billion years ago. These measurements suggest there was a hiatus of almost 5 billion years between the formation of the galactic halo and the thin disk. Recent analysis of the chemical signatures of thousands of stars suggests that stellar formation might have dropped by an order of magnitude at the time of disk formation, 10 to 8 billion years ago, when interstellar gas was too hot to form new stars at the same rate as before.

The satellite galaxies surrounding the Milky Way are not randomly distributed but appear to result from the breakup of a larger system, producing a ring structure 500,000 light-years in diameter and 50,000 light-years wide. Close encounters between galaxies, like that expected in 4 billion years with the Andromeda Galaxy, can rip off huge tails of gas, which, over time can coalesce to form dwarf galaxies in a ring at an arbitrary angle to the main disc.
## Sun's location and neighborhood

The Solar System is located at a radius of about 27,000 light-years (8. 3 kiloparsecs) from the Galactic Center, near the inner edge of the Orion Arm, within the Local Fluff of the Local Bubble, between the Radcliffe wave and Split linear structures (formerly Gould Belt). Based upon studies of stellar orbits around Sgr A* by Gillessen et al. (2016), the Sun lies at an estimated distance of 27. 14 plus or minus 0. 46 kly (8. 32 plus or minus 0. 14 kiloparsecs) from the Galactic Center. Boehle et al. (2016) found a smaller value of 25. 64 plus or minus 0. 46 kly (7. 86 plus or minus 0. 14 kiloparsecs), also using a star orbit analysis. The Sun is currently 5–30 parsecs (16–98 light years) above, or north of, the central plane of the Galactic disk. The distance between the local arm and the next arm out, the Perseus Arm, is about 2,000 parsecs (6,500 light years). The Solar System is located in the Milky Way's galactic habitable zone.

There are about 208 stars brighter than absolute magnitude 8. 5 within a sphere with a radius of 15 parsecs (49 light years) from the Sun, giving a density of one star per 69 cubic parsecs, or one star per 2,360 cubic light-years. On the other hand, there are 64 known stars (of any magnitude, not counting 4 brown dwarfs) within 5 parsecs (16 light years) of the Sun, giving a density of about one star per 8. 2 cubic parsecs, or one per 284 cubic light-years. This illustrates the fact that there are far more faint stars than bright stars: in the entire sky, there are about 500 stars brighter than apparent magnitude 4 but 15. 5 million stars brighter than apparent magnitude 14.

The apex of the Sun's way, or the solar apex, is the direction that the Sun travels through the local standard of rest in the Milky Way. The general direction of the Sun's galactic motion is towards the star Deneb near the constellation of Cygnus, at an angle of roughly 90 sky degrees to the direction of the Galactic Center. The Sun's orbit about the Milky Way is expected to be roughly elliptical, with perturbations from the Galactic spiral arms and non-uniform mass distributions. In addition, the Sun passes through the galactic plane approximately 2. 7 times per orbit. This is similar to how a simple harmonic oscillator works with no drag force (damping) term. These oscillations were until recently thought to coincide with mass lifeform extinction periods on Earth. A reanalysis of the effects of the Sun's transit through the spiral structure based on CO data has failed to find a correlation.

It takes the Solar System about 240 million years to complete one orbit of the Milky Way (a galactic year), so the Sun is thought to have completed 18–20 orbits during its lifetime and 1/1250 of a revolution since the origin of humans. The orbital speed of the Solar System about the center of the Milky Way is approximately 220 kilometres per second (490,000 mph) or 0. 073 percent of the speed of light. The Sun moves through the heliosphere at 84,000 kilometres/h (52,000 mph). At this speed, it takes around 1,400 years for the Solar System to travel a distance of 1 light-year, or 8 days to travel 1 astronomical unit (AU). The Solar System is headed in the direction of the zodiacal constellation Scorpius.
This is where the adapted article ends. The full article, which goes on further, is on Wikipedia.
o-welcome: Welcome to the Cosmologist Library, the audiobook half of Cosmic Sanctuary. Everything here is about one question that people have asked for as long as they have looked up at night: how did it all begin? Not the whole history of the universe up to the present day, which would take years to read, but the first chapter: from the very first instant that physics can talk about, to the time, roughly a billion years later, when the universe was filled with young galaxies, blazing stars and growing black holes. After that, the story becomes the story of galaxies, planets and eventually us, and that is a different library.

The library is arranged in eight sections. The first is the chronology itself: the epochs of the early universe, told in order, from the Planck epoch, when space and time themselves were probably not yet the smooth things we know, through inflation, the forging of particles, the first three minutes when the light elements were cooked, the long glowing fog of plasma, the release of the first light that we still see as the cosmic microwave background, the Dark Ages, the first stars, and the great clearing of the fog called reionisation.

The second section is the physics you need to follow that story. You cannot understand the first second without some feel for relativity, quantum theory, particles and forces, heat and entropy, and the idea of symmetry breaking. These pieces are the umbrella under which the whole story shelters. The third section compares the theories and models of the beginning: the standard Big Bang model with its dark matter and dark energy, inflation and the multiverse it may imply, and rival ideas such as bouncing and cyclic universes, the no-boundary proposal, and Roger Penrose's conformal cyclic cosmology.

The fourth section is the evidence: the things we can measure today that carry the fingerprints of the early universe, from the afterglow of the Big Bang to the amounts of hydrogen, helium and lithium in old stars, the giant pattern of galaxies across the sky, and the extraordinary first galaxies seen by the James Webb Space Telescope. The fifth section is about arguments: the controversies and open problems, presented fairly, with the case on each side. The sixth looks the other way in time, to the end of the universe and the many ways it might come. The seventh is about the instruments, especially radio telescopes, and what they can tell us that ordinary telescopes cannot, along with the detectors that catch gravitational waves and ghostly neutrinos. The eighth looks forward, to the observatories now being built and the discoveries people hope for.

Most of the pieces are articles from Wikipedia, the free encyclopaedia, adapted for listening. References, tables and lists have been taken out, and where an article used a formula, the formula has either been spoken in plain words or left out with a short note. Wikipedia articles are written by many hands, and they can be uneven, but the best of them are superb. Woven between them are original pieces written for this library: an overview at the start of each section, a series called The Story So Far, which carries you from one epoch to the next in plain language, and a set of controversy explainers, which lay out each side of the great arguments without taking sides where the science has not yet decided.

Every piece begins with a spoken title, and where it belongs to a moment in cosmic history, the title begins with that moment, so that you always know where in time you are. Times in the early universe are often given as powers of ten. Ten to the minus thirty-six seconds means a decimal point followed by thirty-five zeros and then a one: a fraction of a second so small that there is nothing in everyday life to compare it with. Ten to the minus six seconds is a millionth of a second. Each step in the power is a factor of ten, so ten to the minus thirty-two seconds is ten thousand times longer than ten to the minus thirty-six. You will soon get used to hearing time this way.

There are four ways to listen. Chronological mode starts at the very beginning and moves forward through cosmic time, bringing in background physics and evidence at the moment they are needed. Thematic mode gathers everything about one big topic, such as dark matter, neutrinos or radio astronomy, from the simplest pieces to the most demanding. Shuffle takes you round and round the universe in a random order, never repeating a piece until you have heard everything you chose. And one section only plays a single section from start to finish. You can also browse the library and read any piece on the screen, mark favourites, and set a sleep timer. If you wish, the soundscape can play quietly underneath the reading, following the era you are hearing about.

A word about certainty. Some of what you will hear is as solid as anything in science: the universe was once hot and dense, it has been expanding and cooling for about thirteen point eight billion years, and the light elements were made in its first few minutes. Some is well supported but still being tested, such as inflation and dark matter. And some, especially the very first moments and anything before them, is honest speculation by the best minds we have. The pieces try to make clear which is which. Enjoy the journey.
o-ov-chrono: The history of the universe is written backwards. We live at the end of it, and everything we know about the beginning has been worked out by looking at light that has travelled for billions of years, and by running the laws of physics in reverse. When we do that, a remarkable picture emerges. The farther back we go, the smaller, denser and hotter everything becomes. Galaxies crowd together, then dissolve into a smooth glowing gas. Atoms are torn apart into nuclei and electrons. Nuclei break into protons and neutrons, and those melt into a soup of quarks and gluons. At still earlier times, even the distinctions between the forces of nature fade away. This section follows that history in the right direction, forwards from the earliest moment we can describe.

Cosmologists divide the early universe into epochs. They are not sharp chapters with clean edges, but convenient names for stretches of time during which one kind of physics was in charge. Here is the whole story in a few minutes, so that you have a map before you set out.

First comes the Planck epoch, the first ten to the minus forty-three seconds. This is where our two best theories, general relativity and quantum mechanics, both claim the territory and contradict each other. Nobody knows what happened here, or even whether time had its ordinary meaning. Next comes the grand unification epoch, when gravity had separated from the other forces but the strong nuclear force, the weak force and electromagnetism may still have been one. Then, at around ten to the minus thirty-six seconds, many cosmologists believe the universe underwent inflation: an astonishingly rapid expansion that stretched a tiny patch to a size larger than everything we can now see, smoothing it, flattening it, and planting the faint ripples that later grew into galaxies. When inflation ended, its energy poured into a hot bath of particles. This is what most cosmologists mean today by the hot Big Bang.

Then came the electroweak epoch, ending at about a trillionth of a second, when the Higgs field settled into its present state and gave mass to the fundamental particles; the weak force and electromagnetism went their separate ways. In the quark epoch that followed, the universe was a plasma of free quarks and gluons, the same strange liquid that is briefly recreated today when heavy atoms are smashed together at the Large Hadron Collider. At about a millionth of a second, it cooled enough for quarks to be locked into protons and neutrons: the hadron epoch. Somewhere in those very early moments, by a process we still do not understand, a tiny excess of matter over antimatter was created. When matter and antimatter annihilated, that small excess, about one part in a billion, was left over. Everything you have ever seen is made of it.

At around one second, the ghostly neutrinos stopped interacting with everything else and streamed away freely; they are still all around us as a cosmic neutrino background. Electrons and positrons annihilated, heating the light. From about ten seconds to twenty minutes, the universe was a nuclear reactor. Protons and neutrons fused into deuterium, helium, and a trace of lithium. The amounts made then are still measured today, and they agree with the theory beautifully. That is one of the great pillars of the Big Bang.

Then a long quiet stretch. For about three hundred and eighty thousand years, the universe was a glowing plasma of nuclei, electrons and light, opaque like the inside of a cloud. Sound waves rang through it. When it cooled to about three thousand degrees, electrons joined nuclei to make the first atoms, and the light was set free. That light, stretched by the expansion of the universe into microwaves, is the cosmic microwave background, the oldest light there is. Its tiny patterns are a photograph of the baby universe.

After the light was released came the Dark Ages, with no stars at all, only cooling gas and invisible dark matter slowly gathering into clumps. After perhaps a hundred million years or so, the first stars ignited in the densest clumps: probably huge, hot and short-lived, made of only hydrogen and helium. Their ultraviolet light, and the light of the first small galaxies and black holes, gradually split the neutral hydrogen gas back into ions. By about a billion years, this reionisation was complete, and the universe was transparent and full of galaxies, quasars powered by enormous black holes, and the heavy elements forged in the first exploding stars. That is where our story ends, at a little later.

In this section you will find The Story So Far, a series of original narrations, one for each epoch, alongside the encyclopaedia articles about each period and the processes that shaped it. In chronological mode, the background physics from other sections will be woven in where it is first needed.
o-s01: Every story needs a first line, and the story of the universe has a problem with its first line. When people say the universe began with the Big Bang, they usually picture an explosion: a tiny point bursting outwards into empty darkness. Almost every part of that picture is wrong, and clearing it away is the best way to begin.

First, there was no empty darkness outside. In the modern picture, the Big Bang did not happen at a place in space. It happened everywhere at once. Space itself was smaller, in the sense that the distances between any two points were shorter, and everything in it was compressed, hot and dense. If the universe is infinite today, as it may well be, then it was infinite at the beginning too, just far denser. What we call the observable universe, everything from which light has had time to reach us, was once squeezed into a region smaller than an atom. But that region was not alone, and it was not an object floating in a void.

Second, it was not an explosion in the ordinary sense. An explosion is driven by a pressure difference: high pressure inside, low pressure outside. In the early universe, the pressure was the same everywhere, so there was nothing to push against. The expansion was not a blast but a stretching of space itself, described by Einstein's general theory of relativity. Galaxies today are not flying through space away from us; they are being carried apart by the space between them growing, like raisins in rising dough.

Third, and most important, the Big Bang theory is really a theory of what happened after the beginning, not of the beginning itself. Run the expansion backwards using general relativity, and the density and temperature rise without limit, until, at a finite time in the past, they become infinite. This point is called the initial singularity. But almost no physicist believes it is real. Infinities in physics usually mean that a theory has been pushed beyond its limits. Long before the singularity is reached, the universe becomes so dense that quantum effects on gravity must matter, and we have no tested theory of quantum gravity. So the honest statement is this: we can trace the history of the universe back to a very hot, dense state with great confidence; we can trace it back further with growing uncertainty; and at the very earliest moment, our theories fall silent.

How confident is confident? It helps to think in layers. From about a hundredth of a second onwards, the physics is the physics of nuclei and particles that we have tested in laboratories, and the predictions, especially the amounts of light elements made in the first minutes, match observations superbly. Back to about a trillionth of a second, the temperatures correspond to energies reached at the Large Hadron Collider, so the physics is known, even if we cannot observe that era directly. Before that, we are extrapolating our theories beyond anything tested, guided by elegance and by the clues the universe left behind. Inflation, which may have happened at around ten to the minus thirty-six seconds, is well supported by indirect evidence but not proven. And before inflation, or before the Planck time, all is speculation.

That is why many cosmologists today use the phrase Big Bang in two different ways. Sometimes it means the first instant, the hypothetical singularity. More often it means the hot, dense, rapidly expanding state from which everything we see emerged. If inflation happened, then that hot state began when inflation ended, and the question of what came before is wide open. Some theories say time itself began. Some say there was a previous contracting universe that bounced. Some say our universe is one bubble in an endlessly inflating multiverse. You will meet all of them in this library.

One more idea will help throughout: the link between time, temperature and energy. As the universe expands, everything in it cools. Light is stretched to longer wavelengths, which means lower energy. So the early universe was hotter the earlier you go, and in the early universe there is a simple rule of thumb: the temperature falls in step with the square root of the time, so if you wait four times as long, it is half as hot. At one second, the temperature was about ten billion degrees. At a hundredth of a second, ten times hotter. And because temperature measures the energy of particles, the hotter it was, the heavier the particles that could be created in collisions. The history of the early universe is therefore a history of cooling, in which, one by one, kinds of particle and kinds of force froze out of the hot soup into the forms we know. The epochs you will hear about in this series are the stages of that freezing. So let us start the clock, at the earliest moment physics dares to name.
o-s02: The first chapter of cosmic history is the one about which we know least. It is called the Planck epoch, and it covers the time from the beginning, whatever that was, to about ten to the minus forty-three seconds. That number, the Planck time, is not arbitrary. It comes from combining three fundamental constants of nature: the speed of light, the strength of gravity, and Planck's constant, which sets the scale of quantum effects. In 1899, the German physicist Max Planck noticed that these constants could be combined to give natural units of length, time, mass and temperature that do not depend on any human choice. The Planck time is the shortest of these: about five times ten to the minus forty-four seconds. The Planck length is about ten to the minus thirty-five metres, around a hundred billion billion times smaller than a proton.

What makes these scales special is that they are where gravity and quantum theory collide. General relativity describes gravity as the smooth curvature of spacetime. Quantum theory says that, on small enough scales, everything fluctuates. Put the two together and, at the Planck scale, the very geometry of space and time should fluctuate wildly. Space might be a foam of tiny bubbles and tunnels. The order of events might not be fixed. Time itself might not exist in any ordinary sense. To describe this, we need a theory of quantum gravity, and we do not have a tested one.

The temperature at the end of the Planck epoch is usually quoted as about ten to the thirty-two degrees, the Planck temperature, though if inflation happened, the universe may never have been this hot, and the Planck epoch may belong to a pre-inflationary phase that we can barely imagine. This is an important point that popular accounts often skip. The traditional chronology simply runs the hot Big Bang backwards to time zero. The modern view, with inflation, places a period of rapid, cold expansion before the hot Big Bang. In that view, the Planck era is not necessarily the first moment of our hot universe, but the frontier at which the inflationary universe itself emerged, from something we cannot yet describe.

What might happen at this frontier? The candidate theories each tell a different story. String theory says the fundamental objects are not points but tiny vibrating strings, and that space may have extra dimensions curled up too small to see. In some string scenarios, our universe is a membrane floating in a higher dimensional space, and the Big Bang was a collision between membranes. Loop quantum gravity says space is made of discrete chunks, woven from loops, and that this granularity prevents the density from ever becoming infinite: a collapsing universe would bounce. Stephen Hawking and James Hartle proposed that, near the beginning, time behaves like a direction in space, so that the universe has no boundary and no first moment, just as the Earth's surface has no edge at the South Pole. Others suggest the universe tunnelled into existence from nothing by a quantum process, or that it emerged from an earlier contracting phase.

It is tempting to dismiss all of this as untestable. But the Planck epoch is not quite out of reach. If inflation happened, it may have stretched quantum fluctuations from near the Planck scale up to the size of galaxies, so the largest structures in the universe could carry faint traces of physics at unimaginably small scales. Gravitational waves from the earliest moments, if they can ever be detected, would come from even earlier, because nothing can stop them. And some theories predict distinctive patterns in the cosmic microwave background, or relics such as cosmic strings, that could in principle be seen.

The physicist John Wheeler liked to say that the Planck scale is where space and time lose their meaning, and he coined the phrase quantum foam for what might lie there. For now, the Planck epoch is less a chapter of history than a sign at the edge of the map saying: here, our knowledge ends. It is a humbling place to start. But as the clock passed ten to the minus forty-three seconds, gravity separated from the other forces, spacetime settled into the smooth stage described by Einstein, and the story enters territory that physics can begin to describe.
o-s03: After the Planck epoch, from about ten to the minus forty-three to ten to the minus thirty-six seconds, comes a period known as the grand unification epoch. Its name comes from a bold idea in particle physics: that three of the four forces of nature, the strong nuclear force, the weak nuclear force and electromagnetism, are really different faces of a single force, which shows its true unified form only at enormous energies.

To understand why physicists believe this, it helps to know what the forces are like today. Electromagnetism holds atoms together, makes light, and governs chemistry. The weak force is responsible for some kinds of radioactivity and for the first step in the fusion that powers the Sun. The strong force binds quarks into protons and neutrons, and holds atomic nuclei together. Today these three are wildly different in strength and character. But in quantum field theory, the strength of a force is not fixed: it changes with the energy at which you probe it. Measurements show that electromagnetism grows stronger at higher energies, while the strong force grows weaker. If you extrapolate, the three forces approach each other, and in some theories they meet at an energy of around ten to the sixteen billion electron volts, about a trillion times higher than anything a particle collider can reach. That meeting point is the grand unification scale, and in the hot early universe, with temperatures around ten to the twenty-eight degrees or more, typical particle energies would have been that high.

We already know that unification of this kind happens. In the 1960s and 1970s, Sheldon Glashow, Abdus Salam and Steven Weinberg showed that electromagnetism and the weak force are united into a single electroweak force at energies above about a hundred billion electron volts. That theory was confirmed in detail, most dramatically when the W and Z particles, carriers of the weak force, were found at CERN in 1983, and finally with the discovery of the Higgs boson in 2012. Grand unified theories, first proposed by Howard Georgi and Glashow in 1974, take the next step and add the strong force.

These theories make striking predictions. One is that quarks and leptons, the two families of matter particles, are related, which means that a quark could turn into a lepton. If so, the proton is not perfectly stable: it should decay, extremely slowly. Huge underground water tanks, such as Super-Kamiokande in Japan, have watched for proton decay for decades without seeing it, which shows the proton lives at least ten to the thirty-four years, and has ruled out the simplest grand unified theory. Another prediction is the existence of magnetic monopoles, particles carrying a single north or south magnetic pole, which would have been made in vast numbers as the unified force broke apart. We have never found one. That absence was one of the puzzles that led to the idea of inflation, which would have diluted the monopoles to the point of invisibility.

So the grand unification epoch is partly a story about theory. If grand unification is right, then at the end of this epoch, as the universe cooled below the unification temperature, the unified force split, the strong force going its own way, in a transition rather like water freezing into ice. Such transitions, called phase transitions, can release energy and leave behind defects: monopoles, strings or walls, like the cracks in a frozen pond. Some physicists have suggested that the energy driving inflation was connected with this transition, though most modern models of inflation treat its driving field, called the inflaton, as something separate.

It is worth saying clearly that we do not know whether grand unification happened. The forces do not quite meet at a single point in the Standard Model alone; they meet more neatly if there are additional particles, such as those predicted by supersymmetry, which the Large Hadron Collider has looked for without success. Grand unification remains an attractive hypothesis, not established fact. But it captures a pattern that runs through the whole early universe: the hotter it was, the simpler and more symmetric physics seems to have been, and the history of the universe is, in part, the history of that symmetry breaking down. The next chapter brings the most dramatic event of all: inflation.
o-s04: At around ten to the minus thirty-six seconds, according to the theory most cosmologists favour, something extraordinary happened. The universe began to expand at an accelerating, exponential rate, doubling in size again and again, perhaps eighty or more times, in a tiny fraction of a second. A region smaller than a proton was stretched to something larger than a grapefruit, or, in many versions, far larger: much bigger than the whole of the universe we can observe today. This was cosmic inflation, and when it ended, perhaps by about ten to the minus thirty-two seconds, it left behind the hot, smooth, expanding universe that the classic Big Bang theory describes.

Why believe something so extreme? Inflation was proposed by the American physicist Alan Guth in 1980, with related ideas developed by Alexei Starobinsky in the Soviet Union, and Guth's motivation was to solve three puzzles. The first is the horizon problem. The cosmic microwave background has the same temperature, to one part in a hundred thousand, in every direction. But in the standard Big Bang, regions on opposite sides of the sky were never close enough to exchange heat; light had not had time to travel between them. How did they come to agree? Inflation answers that they were once very close, inside a tiny region that had time to even out, before inflation stretched them apart. The second puzzle is flatness. Space appears to be almost perfectly flat, neither curved like a sphere nor like a saddle. In the standard theory, any initial curvature grows with time, so the early universe would have needed to be flat to fantastic precision. Inflation flattens space automatically, just as the surface of a balloon looks flatter the more it is blown up. The third puzzle is the absence of relics such as magnetic monopoles, which inflation dilutes away.

What drives inflation? In most models, a field that fills space, called the inflaton, is in a state of high energy, rather like a ball resting on a high plateau. That energy behaves like a form of antigravity, a negative pressure that makes space expand faster and faster. As the inflaton slowly rolls towards the bottom of its hill, inflation continues. When it reaches the bottom, it oscillates and decays, dumping its energy into a hot bath of particles. This is called reheating, and it is the moment when the hot Big Bang, in the modern sense, begins. Guth's original version had a flaw: it ended in a patchwork of bubbles that would have made the universe lumpy. Andrei Linde, and Andreas Albrecht and Paul Steinhardt, fixed this in 1982 with new inflation, and Linde later proposed chaotic inflation, which needs only a simple field.

The greatest triumph of inflation came from an unexpected direction. Quantum mechanics says that no field can be perfectly still; it always jitters. During inflation, those tiny quantum jitters in the inflaton were stretched to enormous sizes and frozen in, becoming slight differences in density from place to place. These differences were the seeds of everything: the hot and cold spots in the microwave background, and, after billions of years of gravity pulling them together, galaxies and clusters of galaxies. Inflation predicts specific properties for these seeds. They should be almost the same strength on all scales, but very slightly stronger on large scales than small ones. They should follow the statistics of a bell curve. And they should be adiabatic, meaning that all components, matter and light, vary together. The Planck satellite confirmed all of these: the tilt towards large scales is measured at about three and a half percent, just as simple inflation models suggest. When you look at a galaxy, inflation says, you are looking at a quantum fluctuation magnified by gravity.

Inflation also predicts that gravitational waves, ripples in spacetime, were generated the same way, and would leave a faint twisting pattern in the polarisation of the microwave background. These have not yet been found. Their absence so far has ruled out some of the simplest models, such as inflation driven by a field with a plain squared energy, and favours models in which the inflaton's energy flattens out, such as Starobinsky's original idea. The hunt continues with the Simons Observatory, the BICEP and Keck experiments and, in future, the LiteBIRD satellite.

Inflation has critics, including some of its own founders. Paul Steinhardt now argues that inflation is so flexible that it can be tuned to fit any observation, and that in most versions it becomes eternal, producing a multiverse in which anything that can happen does happen infinitely often, so that it predicts nothing. Supporters reply that specific models make sharp predictions that have already been tested. You will hear both sides in the controversies section. But either way, after inflation, the universe was hot, dense, almost perfectly smooth, and filled with an unimaginably energetic soup of particles. The age of particle physics had begun.
o-s05: When inflation ended and the universe reheated, it was filled with a seething soup of particles at a temperature of perhaps ten to the twenty-seven degrees or more, the exact figure depending on the details of inflation that we do not yet know. From then until about a trillionth of a second, cosmologists speak of the electroweak epoch. Its name tells us what was special about it: electromagnetism and the weak nuclear force had not yet separated. They acted as one electroweak force.

What would that soup have been like? Every kind of particle in the Standard Model was present, constantly created and destroyed in collisions: quarks of all six kinds, including the heavy top quark; electrons and their heavier cousins the muon and the tau; the three kinds of neutrino; gluons, which carry the strong force; and the carriers of the electroweak force. And there was one more crucial feature. All of these particles were massless. In the electroweak epoch, electrons, quarks and the carriers of the weak force all moved at the speed of light, like photons do today.

This sounds strange, because mass seems such a basic property. But in the Standard Model, the fundamental particles do not have mass on their own. They get it by interacting with the Higgs field, an invisible field that fills all space. The idea was proposed in 1964 by Peter Higgs, and independently by François Englert and Robert Brout, and by Gerald Guralnik, Carl Hagen and Tom Kibble. Here is a picture that helps. Imagine the Higgs field as a kind of treacle filling space. Particles that interact strongly with it, such as the top quark, are slowed a great deal and become heavy; particles that interact weakly, such as the electron, become light; the photon does not interact with it at all, and stays massless. This picture is imperfect, because the Higgs field does not cause friction, but it captures the idea that mass comes from interaction.

The key is that, at very high temperatures, the Higgs field sat at zero on average, in a symmetric state. Its potential energy is often described as shaped like the bottom of a wine bottle, or a Mexican hat: a hump in the middle and a circular valley around it. When the universe was hot, the field effectively sat on top of the hump, and the symmetry between electromagnetism and the weak force was intact. As the universe cooled to a temperature of about ten to the fifteen degrees, at around a trillionth of a second, the hump became the high ground, and the field rolled down into the valley, everywhere in the universe. It took on a non-zero value, which it has kept ever since. In that moment, the electroweak symmetry broke. The W and Z particles, carriers of the weak force, became heavy, about eighty-six and ninety-seven times the mass of a proton, which is why the weak force is so weak and short-ranged today. The photon remained massless, and electromagnetism became the long-range force we know. And the quarks and electrons acquired their masses. Physicists call this electroweak symmetry breaking.

How do we know? Because we have recreated these conditions. The Large Hadron Collider at CERN, near Geneva, smashes protons together at energies that correspond to the temperatures of the electroweak epoch. In 2012, its two great experiments, ATLAS and CMS, announced the discovery of the Higgs boson, a ripple in the Higgs field, with a mass about a hundred and thirty-three times that of a proton. Peter Higgs and François Englert received the Nobel prize in 2013. Since then, measurements have shown that the Higgs boson interacts with other particles in proportion to their masses, just as the theory requires.

There are still mysteries here. According to calculations using the measured Higgs mass, the electroweak transition in the Standard Model was not a sudden jump, like water boiling, but a smooth crossover. That matters, because a sudden, violent transition, with bubbles of the new phase expanding and colliding, could have produced gravitational waves we might detect with LISA, and could have helped create the excess of matter over antimatter. In the Standard Model alone, it seems neither happened. Many physicists suspect there are extra particles that would make the transition more dramatic. Another puzzle is why the Higgs mass is so small compared with the scales of grand unification and gravity; this is called the hierarchy problem. And measurements of the Higgs and the top quark suggest that the valley in which the Higgs field sits may not be the lowest possible: our vacuum might be only metastable, a possibility you will meet in the section on the end of the universe.

By about a trillionth of a second, then, the universe had its familiar forces and its massive particles. But it was still far too hot for quarks to stick together. The next chapter is the quark epoch.
o-s06: From about a trillionth of a second to about a millionth of a second after the beginning, the universe passed through what is called the quark epoch. The forces had taken their present forms, and the particles had their masses, but the temperature, falling from about ten to the fifteen degrees to a few trillion degrees, was still far too high for quarks to be bound into protons and neutrons. The universe was filled with a quark gluon plasma.

Quarks are the building blocks of protons and neutrons. Each proton contains two up quarks and one down quark; each neutron one up and two down. They are held together by the strong force, carried by particles called gluons. The strong force has a peculiar property. Most forces grow weaker with distance, but the strong force between quarks does not; if you try to pull two quarks apart, the energy in the gluon field between them grows until it is enough to create a new pair of quarks, so you never get a lone quark, just more particles. This is called confinement, and it is why we never see a free quark today. But the strong force also has the opposite property at short distances, or high energies: quarks very close together barely feel it at all. David Gross, Frank Wilczek and David Politzer discovered this in 1973, calling it asymptotic freedom, and won the Nobel prize in 2004. In the quark epoch, the universe was so hot and dense that quarks and gluons were constantly jostled close together, and moved freely through the plasma, no longer locked inside particles.

Physicists once imagined that such a plasma would be a thin gas of particles flying freely. The reality, discovered at the Relativistic Heavy Ion Collider in New York in the early two thousands, and confirmed at the Large Hadron Collider, was a surprise. When gold or lead nuclei are smashed together at nearly the speed of light, they create a tiny droplet of quark gluon plasma, at temperatures of several trillion degrees, more than a hundred thousand times hotter than the centre of the Sun. That droplet behaves not like a gas but like a liquid, and an almost perfect one, flowing with less internal friction, relative to its density, than any other substance known. The early universe, for a few millionths of a second, was filled with this perfect liquid.

The plasma contained more than quarks and gluons. Electrons, muons, neutrinos and photons all swarmed through it, along with antiparticles of each kind. Matter and antimatter were present in almost equal amounts, constantly annihilating into light and being recreated from it. But not quite equal. At some point, perhaps during the electroweak transition, perhaps earlier, a tiny excess of quarks over antiquarks had appeared: roughly one extra quark for every billion pairs. Nobody knows how. The process, whatever it was, is called baryogenesis, and it is one of the deepest open problems in physics. All that matters for the story is that the excess was there, and that it would decide the future of everything.

During the quark epoch, the heaviest particles began to disappear. The top quark, the bottom quark, the W and Z bosons and the Higgs boson are all heavy and unstable. While the universe was hot enough, collisions created them as fast as they decayed. As it cooled, typical collisions no longer had enough energy to make them, and they vanished from the soup, decaying into lighter particles. This pattern, a particle staying common while the temperature exceeds its mass, then dying out, repeats again and again through the early universe. Cosmologists sometimes say that particles freeze out.

Could there be relics of this era today? Possibly. If the transition from quark plasma to ordinary matter had been violent, it could have made primordial black holes or gravitational waves; calculations suggest it was actually a smooth crossover, though a slight change in conditions could have made it more dramatic. Some physicists have proposed exotic lumps of quark matter, called strangelets or quark nuggets, as a form of dark matter, though there is no evidence for them. And the gravitational wave background found by pulsar timing arrays in 2023 has prompted some to ask whether it could come from events around this time, though the more conventional explanation is pairs of giant black holes in the present universe.

At about a millionth of a second, the temperature dropped to around two trillion degrees, and the quark epoch ended. Quarks and gluons condensed into protons, neutrons and other particles, an event called hadronisation. That is the next chapter.
o-s07: At about a millionth of a second after the beginning, the temperature of the universe fell to around two trillion degrees, and something fundamental changed. Quarks and gluons could no longer roam free. They condensed into composite particles called hadrons, a family that includes protons and neutrons, as well as short-lived particles such as pions. This marks the start of the hadron epoch, which lasted until about one second.

The change from quark plasma to hadrons is called hadronisation, or the quark hadron transition. Modern calculations, using supercomputers to solve the equations of the strong force on a grid of points in space and time, a technique called lattice quantum chromodynamics, indicate that it happened smoothly rather than suddenly, a crossover rather than a boiling, at a temperature corresponding to about a hundred and fifty million electron volts. Laboratory experiments with colliding heavy nuclei agree: when the droplet of plasma created in a collision expands and cools, it turns into a spray of ordinary particles with the proportions that this temperature predicts.

Once the hadrons formed, they did what the quarks had done before: matter and antimatter annihilated. At first, the universe was hot enough for collisions between photons to create pairs of protons and antiprotons, and neutrons and antineutrons, as fast as they destroyed each other. But the mass of a proton corresponds to a temperature of about ten trillion degrees, and the universe was already cooler than that. Pairs could no longer be created as fast as they annihilated, and within a fraction of the hadron epoch, nearly all the protons and antiprotons, and neutrons and antineutrons, were gone, turned into light. What remained was the tiny excess: about one proton or neutron for every billion or so photons. That ratio, measured today from the cosmic microwave background and the light elements, is one of the most important numbers in cosmology. It means that the universe today contains roughly a billion photons of the microwave background for every atom. Everything made of ordinary matter, stars, planets, people, is the leftover from a nearly perfect cancellation.

Lighter hadrons, such as pions, lasted a little longer, but they too decayed or annihilated as the temperature fell. By about one second, the hadrons that remained were essentially protons and neutrons, in a sea of electrons, positrons, neutrinos and light. And the balance between protons and neutrons had begun to matter. While the universe was hot, protons and neutrons constantly turned into each other through the weak force, by colliding with electrons, positrons and neutrinos. Because a neutron is very slightly heavier than a proton, about a tenth of a percent, it takes a little energy to make one, and as the temperature fell, protons became more common than neutrons. This shifting balance would decide how much helium the universe would make in its first minutes.

Is there anything from this era still around? Possibly black holes. If the density in some regions was high enough, they might have collapsed directly into primordial black holes, with masses depending on the time they formed. Black holes formed during the hadron epoch would have masses similar to that of the Sun. Some researchers have suggested that the black holes seen colliding by gravitational wave detectors could include some of these, or that primordial black holes could make up part of the dark matter. Observations have ruled out many mass ranges, but some windows remain open. It is an active area of research, and an example of how the very early universe could have left relics we might still find.

The hadron epoch also brings us within reach of experiment in a second way. The temperature of the universe at its end, about ten billion degrees, corresponds to energies routinely studied in nuclear physics. From here on, the physics is not extrapolation but well tested laboratory science, and the predictions become very precise. That is why cosmologists are so confident about what happened next. At about one second, the neutrinos broke away from everything else, and the universe entered the lepton epoch.
o-s08: At about one second after the beginning, the universe was a ball of radiation and light particles at roughly ten billion degrees. Protons and neutrons were now a tiny minority, about one for every billion photons. Most of the energy was carried by photons, by electrons and their antimatter twins, positrons, and by neutrinos. Electrons, positrons and neutrinos belong to a family of particles called leptons, and so this period, from about one second to about ten seconds, is called the lepton epoch.

The first great event of the lepton epoch, happening right at its start, was neutrino decoupling. Neutrinos are the most elusive particles known. They have no electric charge and feel only the weak force and gravity, so they pass through ordinary matter almost as if it were not there; trillions of neutrinos from the Sun pass through your body every second without effect. In the first second, however, the universe was so dense that even neutrinos were constantly colliding with electrons and positrons, sharing their energy and staying at the same temperature as everything else. As the universe expanded and thinned, collisions became rarer. At about one second, at a temperature of around ten billion degrees, the time between collisions became longer than the age of the universe. The neutrinos stopped interacting and streamed away freely. They have been travelling ever since, cooling as the universe expands.

Those neutrinos should still be everywhere, about three hundred and thirty of them in every cubic centimetre of space, forming a cosmic neutrino background, a counterpart to the microwave background but released at one second rather than three hundred and eighty thousand years. Their temperature today should be about one point nine five degrees above absolute zero. Detecting them directly is fantastically difficult, because they are so cold and interact so weakly; a proposed experiment called PTOLEMY aims to try one day. But we can see their influence. They contributed to the expansion rate in the first minutes, affecting how much helium was made, and they left measurable imprints in the microwave background and in the pattern of galaxies. Measurements from Planck show that the number of neutrino-like species present in the early universe is very close to the three we know: a beautiful confirmation that the story is right back to one second.

The second great event was the annihilation of electrons and positrons. While the temperature was above about six billion degrees, collisions between photons created electron positron pairs as fast as they annihilated. As the universe cooled further, pair creation stopped, and the electrons and positrons destroyed each other, leaving, once again, a small excess of electrons: just enough to balance the electric charge of the protons. The energy of all those annihilations went into the photons, heating them. But the neutrinos had already decoupled and did not share in this heating. That is why the neutrino background today is cooler than the microwave background: one point nine five degrees compared with two point seven three. The ratio between those temperatures can be calculated exactly from the physics of the annihilation, and the effect of the extra heating shows up clearly in precise measurements of the early universe.

Meanwhile, the balance between neutrons and protons was settling. At around one second, the weak interactions that turned protons into neutrons and back again became too slow to keep up with the expansion, at about the same time as the neutrinos decoupled. The ratio froze at about one neutron for every six protons. After that, the only change was that free neutrons, which are unstable, began to decay into protons, with a half-life of about ten minutes. The universe now had a race against time: the neutrons needed to be locked safely inside nuclei before too many of them decayed.

By about ten seconds, the temperature had fallen to around three billion degrees, most of the electrons and positrons were gone, and the energy of the universe was dominated by photons, with neutrinos as a cold, silent companion. The lepton epoch was over, and the photon epoch had begun. Within a few minutes, the universe would become a nuclear furnace.
o-s09: In 1977, the physicist Steven Weinberg published a short, beautiful book called The First Three Minutes. Its title captured one of the most remarkable achievements of science: we can describe what happened in the universe between a few seconds and about twenty minutes after the beginning in great detail, and test it against measurements made today. This period is called Big Bang nucleosynthesis, the making of the first atomic nuclei.

At about ten seconds, the universe was a hot, dense mixture of photons, neutrinos, protons, neutrons and electrons, with about one neutron for every six or seven protons. To build a nucleus heavier than a single proton, the first step is to combine one proton and one neutron into a deuteron, the nucleus of heavy hydrogen, or deuterium. That reaction happens easily, but at first it was immediately undone. Deuterium is fragile; it is held together only weakly, and the universe was full of energetic photons that smashed each deuteron apart as soon as it formed. Because there were about a billion photons for every proton, even when the typical photon was too weak, there were enough exceptional ones to keep breaking deuterium. This is called the deuterium bottleneck.

The bottleneck broke at about three minutes, when the temperature had fallen to about a billion degrees. Suddenly deuterium could survive, and a cascade of reactions followed very quickly. Deuterons combined with protons and neutrons, and with each other, to make tritium and helium three, and then helium four, the ordinary helium of party balloons. Helium four is very tightly bound, so almost every neutron that still existed ended up inside a helium nucleus. A tiny amount of lithium seven, and even less beryllium, was also made. But there the process stopped. There is no stable nucleus with five or eight particles, so it was very hard to build anything heavier, and the universe was cooling and thinning too fast for the slow reactions needed to jump the gap. Heavier elements would have to wait hundreds of millions of years, for the first stars.

By about twenty minutes, the temperature had fallen too far for any more fusion, and the composition of the universe was fixed. By mass, about seventy-five percent hydrogen and about twenty-five percent helium four. Then traces: deuterium at about twenty-five atoms for every million hydrogen atoms, helium three at a similar level, and lithium at a few parts in ten billion. These numbers can be calculated precisely, and they depend mainly on one quantity: the density of ordinary matter, or more precisely the ratio of protons and neutrons to photons.

This is where the magic happens. Astronomers can measure the primordial amounts of these elements. Helium is measured in clouds of ionised gas in small galaxies that have made few stars. Deuterium, the most sensitive measure, is found in clouds of gas between us and distant quasars, which absorb a little of the quasar's light at a telltale wavelength. Because stars destroy deuterium rather than making it, any deuterium we see must be left over from the first minutes. The measurements agree with the predictions, and they give a value for the density of ordinary matter. Then, completely independently, the cosmic microwave background, released three hundred and eighty thousand years later and governed by entirely different physics, gives another value for the same quantity. The two agree to within a few percent. It is hard to overstate how impressive this is. Two different kinds of physics, at two different times, measured with completely different methods, point to the same number.

And that number held a shock. It shows that ordinary matter, made of protons and neutrons, accounts for only about five percent of the total energy of the universe, and only about a sixth of all matter. Most of the matter in the universe must be something else, something that did not take part in the nuclear reactions of the first minutes: dark matter.

There is one blemish. The predicted amount of lithium seven is about three times more than astronomers find in the oldest stars in our galaxy. This cosmological lithium problem has persisted for decades. It may be that the stars have destroyed some of their lithium, or that the nuclear reaction rates are slightly off, or, more excitingly, that there is new physics. But it does not undermine the overall picture, which is one of the great pillars of the Big Bang. After twenty minutes, the furnace went out, and the universe entered a long, quiet era of glowing plasma.
o-s10: After the first twenty minutes, the universe entered a long chapter, lasting about three hundred and eighty thousand years, that is often passed over quickly, but in which something wonderful happened: the universe rang with sound.

At the start of this era, the universe was a plasma: a hot gas of hydrogen and helium nuclei and free electrons, filled with light. It was too hot for electrons to stay attached to nuclei, so there were no neutral atoms. Light could not travel far, because photons kept bouncing off the free electrons, a process called Thomson scattering. If you could have been there, you would have been inside a glowing fog, bright and featureless in every direction, like the inside of a cloud lit by the Sun, or the inside of a star. The temperature fell steadily, from a billion degrees at the end of nucleosynthesis to a few thousand degrees at the end of this era.

For the first fifty thousand years or so, the energy of the universe was dominated by radiation. But radiation thins out faster than matter as the universe expands, because each photon is not only spread out but also stretched to lower energy. At about fifty thousand years, the density of matter overtook that of radiation. Cosmologists call this matter-radiation equality, and it matters because, from then on, gravity could pull matter together much more effectively. Dark matter, which feels gravity but not light, began to collect in the slightly denser regions planted by inflation.

Ordinary matter tried to follow, but it could not simply fall in. The plasma of ordinary matter and light was bound together tightly, and the light provided an enormous pressure. When gravity pulled the plasma into a denser region, the pressure of the light pushed it back out. The result was oscillation: the plasma fell in, bounced out, fell in again. These oscillations were sound waves. They travelled through the plasma at more than half the speed of light. Across the whole universe, from every initial clump, sound waves rippled outwards. The cosmologist Wayne Hu has made recordings of what these waves would sound like, stretched into the range of human hearing: a deep, rising roar, like a jet passing overhead. The pitch is set by the physics of the plasma, and the pattern of tones is a record of what the universe contained.

Here is the most beautiful part. Each sound wave carried ordinary matter outwards from its starting point, while the dark matter stayed behind. When the plasma eventually turned into neutral atoms and the light was freed, the sound waves stopped dead, frozen in place. The matter they had carried was left in a shell, about four hundred and fifty thousand light years in radius at the time, around each initial clump. Since then, the universe has expanded about eleven hundred times, and the shell has grown to about five hundred million light years. This is the baryon acoustic oscillation scale, and it is imprinted in two places: as a pattern of peaks in the hot and cold spots of the cosmic microwave background, and as a slight preference for galaxies to be separated by about five hundred million light years. In effect, the early universe left a ruler of known size across the sky, and astronomers use it to measure the history of cosmic expansion.

The sound waves also tell us what the universe is made of. The relative heights of the peaks in the microwave background depend on how much ordinary matter was loading the waves, and how much dark matter was providing the gravitational wells. If there were no dark matter, the pattern would look completely different. The measurements show clearly that dark matter outweighed ordinary matter by about five to one, and that it was there, as a separate substance, three hundred and eighty thousand years after the beginning. This is one of the strongest pieces of evidence that dark matter is a real thing and not just a modification of gravity.

Throughout this era, the plasma was cooling. By about three hundred and eighty thousand years, the temperature had fallen to about three thousand degrees, roughly that of the surface of a cool red star. At that temperature, something new became possible. Electrons could finally settle into orbit around nuclei, and the fog began to clear. The next chapter is the release of the first light.
o-s11: About three hundred and eighty thousand years after the beginning, the universe changed from an opaque fog into a transparent gas, and the light that was set free at that moment is still arriving at Earth today, from every direction in the sky. It is the cosmic microwave background, the oldest light in the universe, and the event that released it is called recombination.

The name is a little misleading, because electrons and nuclei had never been combined before; but physicists borrowed the word from the laboratory, where ions and electrons recombine. Here is what happened. As the plasma cooled, electrons were increasingly able to settle into orbit around hydrogen and helium nuclei to form neutral atoms. Helium, which holds its electrons more tightly, went first, at higher temperatures. Hydrogen took longer. You might expect hydrogen atoms to form as soon as the temperature fell below the energy needed to tear an electron away, which corresponds to more than a hundred thousand degrees. But again, there were about a billion photons for every atom, and even when the average photon was too weak, the energetic minority kept ionising any atom that formed. Only when the temperature fell to about three thousand degrees did the number of energetic photons drop enough for atoms to survive. Even then, recombination was surprisingly slow and subtle, because each time an electron dropped into an atom, it released a photon that could ionise another atom nearby. The process depended on the rare ways that atoms could get rid of that energy without it being reabsorbed.

As atoms formed, free electrons disappeared, and photons stopped scattering. They began to travel in straight lines, unimpeded, and the universe became transparent. Physicists call this decoupling, because the light and the matter went their separate ways. The moment, spread over tens of thousands of years, from which the light we see last bounced off an electron, is called the surface of last scattering. Looking out into space is looking back in time, and when we look far enough, in every direction, we see this surface: a glowing wall at a temperature of three thousand degrees, behind which we cannot see with light.

Except that it does not look like three thousand degrees. Since recombination, the universe has expanded about eleven hundred times, and the light has been stretched by the same factor. Its glow, which began as an orange-yellow light like that of a candle flame, is now in the microwave part of the spectrum, with a temperature of two point seven two five degrees above absolute zero. Old analogue televisions, tuned between stations, hissed with a snowy static of which perhaps one percent was this ancient light.

The microwave background has a spectrum that is almost perfectly that of a so-called black body, the glow of an object in perfect thermal equilibrium. The COBE satellite measured it in 1990, and the graph of its data, presented to a meeting of the American Astronomical Society, received a standing ovation; the data points sat exactly on the theoretical curve, with error bars smaller than the thickness of the line. That perfection is very hard to explain in any theory except one in which the universe was once hot and dense, and in equilibrium.

And then there are the patterns. The temperature of the microwave background varies across the sky by only about one part in a hundred thousand. These tiny differences are the imprint of the density variations planted by inflation and shaped by the sound waves of the plasma era. Slightly denser regions were also slightly hotter, but their light had to climb out of a slightly deeper gravitational well, which made it look cooler; the balance of such effects produces the pattern we see. The size of the most common hot and cold spots, about one degree across, twice the width of the full Moon, shows that space is flat. The relative strengths of the following peaks measure the amount of ordinary matter and dark matter, and the overall pattern gives the age of the universe, thirteen point eight billion years, to within about twenty million years. The light is also slightly polarised, a further source of information, and the polarisation pattern from later times tells us when the first stars reionised the universe.

The light also carries the imprint of everything it has passed through on its long journey: the bending of its paths by the gravity of intervening galaxy clusters, which allows maps of dark matter to be made; and slight boosts in energy as it passes through the hot gas in clusters of galaxies. The microwave background is the single richest source of information in cosmology. But at the moment it was released, the universe became dark. The glow faded into the infrared as the universe expanded, and there were not yet any stars. The Dark Ages had begun.
o-s12: After the first light was released, the universe went dark. For perhaps a hundred million years, from about three hundred and eighty thousand years after the beginning until the first stars began to shine, there was no source of visible light anywhere. Cosmologists call this period the cosmic Dark Ages.

At first, the darkness was not total. The leftover glow of the hot plasma filled the universe, at first orange, then red, then, as the expansion stretched it, slipping into the infrared, invisible to human eyes after a few million years. If you had floated through the universe a few million years after recombination, you would have seen nothing at all: a cold, dark, almost perfectly uniform gas of hydrogen and helium atoms, thinning steadily as space expanded.

Yet this was a time of quiet preparation. The density variations planted by inflation were still there, imprinted in both the dark matter and the gas. Dark matter, which had been free of the pressure of light, had already begun to gather into the denser regions even during the plasma era. Now the ordinary gas, released from the grip of the light, could fall into the same regions. Gravity is a patient amplifier: a region slightly denser than average pulls in more matter, becomes denser still, and pulls even harder. Over tens of millions of years, small clumps of dark matter collapsed, and the gas fell in with them.
