In the standard cold dark matter picture, the smallest clumps formed first, merging over time into larger ones, a process called hierarchical structure formation. The clumps, called dark matter haloes, would become the cradles of the first stars and galaxies.

The temperature of the gas is an interesting story in itself. For the first few million years after recombination, a small fraction of free electrons left over from incomplete recombination kept the gas in thermal contact with the microwave background, at the same temperature. But as the universe thinned, that contact was lost, and the gas, now on its own, cooled faster than the background radiation, because a gas of atoms cools faster than light when it expands. So by about fifty million years, the hydrogen gas was colder than the radiation passing through it.

This difference in temperatures is the key to one of the most exciting projects in astronomy: listening to the Dark Ages. A hydrogen atom has a tiny property called spin. Both the proton and the electron behave like tiny magnets, and they can be aligned or opposed. When the electron flips from one alignment to the other, the atom emits or absorbs radio waves with a wavelength of twenty-one centimetres. This is called the hydrogen line, and it was predicted in 1944 by the Dutch astronomer Hendrik van de Hulst and first detected in 1951. In the Dark Ages, cold hydrogen gas would have absorbed a little of the background radiation at this wavelength. Because the universe has expanded since then, the absorption would now appear at much longer wavelengths, metres long, corresponding to radio frequencies of a few tens of megahertz. And because different wavelengths come from different times, mapping this signal across frequencies would be like taking a three-dimensional scan of the universe through the Dark Ages, with vastly more information than the microwave background.

The difficulty is staggering. The signal is perhaps a hundred thousand times fainter than the radio noise from our own galaxy at the same frequencies, and Earth's atmosphere and human transmitters make things worse. For the Dark Ages proper, the best place to listen would be the far side of the Moon, shielded from Earth's radio noise. Several space agencies are studying lunar radio telescopes for exactly this purpose; China's Chang'e missions have already carried low frequency radio experiments, and NASA has studied a radio telescope in a lunar crater.

The Dark Ages are the least explored epoch of cosmic history. We know their beginning from the microwave background, and we are starting to see their end, the cosmic dawn, with the James Webb Space Telescope. But the long middle remains unseen. In it, gravity was quietly building the scaffolding of everything to come. Somewhere, in the densest clump, gas was falling inwards, compressing and heating, and about to do something that had never happened before.
o-s13: Somewhere around a hundred million years after the beginning, perhaps a little earlier, the first star switched on. Nobody saw it. Nobody has yet seen any of the very first stars directly. But astronomers and computer simulations have built a vivid picture of what they were like, and it is very different from the stars we know.

The first stars formed inside small clumps of dark matter, haloes about a million times the mass of the Sun, in which gas had gathered and begun to collapse. For a cloud of gas to collapse into a star, it has to cool; otherwise, the heat produced by compression creates a pressure that halts the collapse. In today's universe, gas cools easily, because it contains heavier elements and dust that radiate heat away. But the first gas contained only hydrogen and helium, with a trace of lithium, the products of the first three minutes. Pure hydrogen and helium are poor coolants. The only way the first clouds could cool was through a small amount of molecular hydrogen, two hydrogen atoms bound together, which formed slowly with the help of the few free electrons left over from recombination. Molecular hydrogen could cool the gas to only a few hundred degrees, much warmer than the coldest clouds today.

That warmth had a big consequence. Warmer gas resists collapse more strongly, so it collapses only in larger clumps. The first stars are therefore thought to have been massive, typically tens of times the mass of the Sun, and some perhaps hundreds of times. Astronomers call them Population Three stars, a name that comes from a historical accident: the stars of our galaxy were first sorted into Population One, the young, metal-rich stars like the Sun, and Population Two, the old, metal-poor stars of the halo, so the hypothetical first stars, with no metals at all, became Population Three. In astronomy, any element heavier than helium is called a metal.

Such stars would have been extraordinarily hot, with surfaces at around a hundred thousand degrees, many times hotter than the Sun, and would have blazed with ultraviolet light. They would also have lived fast and died young, burning through their fuel in just a few million years. Their deaths would have been spectacular. Many would have collapsed into black holes. Some, between about a hundred and forty and two hundred and sixty times the mass of the Sun, would have died in a strange kind of explosion called a pair instability supernova, which blows the whole star apart and leaves nothing behind. In their cores and their explosions, the first stars forged the first carbon, oxygen, silicon, iron and other heavy elements, and scattered them into space. From then on, every new generation of stars would be born from gas enriched with these elements. Even a tiny amount of heavy elements changes star formation: the gas cools more easily, so smaller stars like the Sun can form.

Recent simulations have complicated the picture. They suggest that the collapsing gas often fragmented into several stars, so the first stars were born in small groups, with a range of masses, and that some smaller first stars might, in principle, have survived to the present day. Astronomers have searched for them among the stars of our galaxy, finding some with astonishingly low amounts of heavy elements, less than a ten-millionth of the Sun's. These are not quite first generation stars, but they may be their direct children, carrying the chemical fingerprints of a single first-generation supernova.

Finding the first stars themselves is a goal of the James Webb Space Telescope. In 2023 and 2024, astronomers reported possible hints, such as unusual helium emission from a galaxy at a redshift above ten, but no confirmed detection yet; individual first stars would be far too faint to see, and only a cluster of them, or a gravitationally magnified one, would be visible. The radio signal of hydrogen offers another route. When the first stars switched on, their ultraviolet light changed the state of the hydrogen gas around them, which should produce a distinctive absorption signal at radio frequencies around seventy megahertz. In 2018, the EDGES experiment in Western Australia reported just such a signal, but twice as strong as expected, prompting exotic explanations involving dark matter. A later experiment, SARAS three in India, found no sign of it in 2022. The cosmic dawn signal remains one of the great prizes of radio astronomy.

With the first stars, the universe was no longer dark. Light had returned, in the form of brilliant blue-white beacons scattered across the cosmos, inside the first tiny galaxies. And that light was about to transform the universe once again.
o-s14: The first stars and galaxies did more than light up the universe. Their intense ultraviolet light began to tear apart the hydrogen atoms that filled space, splitting them back into protons and electrons. This process, which began around a hundred million years after the beginning and was essentially complete by about a billion years, is called the epoch of reionisation. It was the last great change in the state of the universe as a whole, and it is one of the hottest topics in astronomy today.

Picture it like this. Around each young galaxy, the ultraviolet light carved out a bubble of ionised gas, glowing faintly and expanding as more stars formed. At first the bubbles were small and isolated, like the first holes in a slice of Swiss cheese. As more galaxies formed, the bubbles grew and began to overlap, until eventually they merged and the whole universe was ionised. Between the galaxies, the gas became hot, around ten thousand degrees or more, and very thin. Today, almost all the hydrogen between the galaxies is still ionised. The universe has stayed reionised ever since.

You might wonder: if ionised gas made the early universe opaque, why didn't reionisation make it opaque again? The answer is that by then, the universe had expanded so much that the gas was far thinner. Light from distant galaxies could pass through the ionised gas with only a little scattering. In fact, the scattering that did occur left a measurable mark on the microwave background, by slightly smoothing its pattern on small scales and adding a faint polarisation on large scales. From this, the Planck satellite worked out that reionisation was about halfway done at about seven or eight hundred million years after the beginning.

The other main evidence comes from quasars, the brilliant cores of distant galaxies powered by giant black holes. Their light, travelling towards us, passes through the intergalactic gas. Any neutral hydrogen absorbs the light at a particular ultraviolet wavelength, shifted to longer wavelengths by the expansion. In 1965, James Gunn and Bruce Peterson predicted that, if the gas were neutral, this absorption would be total, leaving a deep trough in the spectrum. For decades, quasar spectra showed no such trough, meaning the gas was ionised. Then, in 2001, the Sloan Digital Sky Survey found quasars at distances corresponding to about nine hundred million years after the beginning whose spectra did show the trough. Astronomers had reached the tail end of reionisation. Even later, at around a billion years, patchy islands of neutral gas seem to have survived, showing that reionisation ended unevenly.

What caused it? The obvious candidates are the first galaxies, with their hot young stars, and the first quasars, with their growing black holes. Most astronomers had thought galaxies were the main cause, with small, faint galaxies providing most of the ultraviolet light. One of the surprises from the James Webb Space Telescope is that early galaxies seem to produce ionising light more efficiently than expected, and that there are many small active black holes in the young universe, so much so that some researchers have worried about a photon budget crisis: too much ionising light, which would have finished reionisation too early. Resolving this, by understanding how much of the light actually escaped from galaxies into intergalactic space, is an active debate.

Reionisation also shaped the galaxies themselves. Heating the intergalactic gas to ten thousand degrees made it harder for the smallest dark matter haloes to hold onto their gas, which may have stifled star formation in the tiniest galaxies. This may help explain why our Milky Way has fewer small satellite galaxies than simple simulations of dark matter predict.

The ultimate tool for studying reionisation is the twenty-one centimetre radio signal of hydrogen. Where the gas was neutral, it glows or absorbs at this wavelength; where it was ionised, it is silent. A radio map at the right frequencies, between about a hundred and two hundred megahertz, would show the bubbles directly, growing and merging. Arrays such as LOFAR in Europe, the Murchison Widefield Array in Australia and HERA in South Africa have set ever tighter limits on the signal, and the low frequency Square Kilometre Array in Western Australia, now being built, is designed to make the first maps. When it does, we will be able to watch the universe light up, bubble by bubble.
o-s15: By about a billion years after the beginning, the universe had become recognisably like the one we know. It was smaller and denser, about seven times smaller in every direction than today, but it was filled with galaxies, blazing with newly formed stars, dusty with heavy elements, and anchored by black holes, some of them already monstrously large. This is where our story of the early universe ends: at a little later, as the cosmos settled into the long era of galaxies that leads, eventually, to us.

The first galaxies were small, irregular and messy. In the cold dark matter picture, they grew by merging: small clumps of dark matter and gas collided and combined, again and again, building larger systems. Streams of cold gas flowed along the filaments of the cosmic web into the growing galaxies, feeding fierce bursts of star formation. These young galaxies looked nothing like the elegant spirals of today. They were clumpy, turbulent, and often compact, with stars forming many times faster than in the Milky Way now.

The James Webb Space Telescope, launched on Christmas Day 2021 and observing since mid 2022, has transformed our view of this era. Its infrared eyes can see light from the first galaxies that has been stretched out of the visible range by the expansion. Within weeks of its first images, candidates appeared for galaxies far earlier than expected. Many early claims turned out to be mistaken, as dusty, closer galaxies masqueraded as distant ones, but many others were confirmed by taking spectra. In 2024, the JADES team confirmed a galaxy, JADES G S z fourteen zero, seen about two hundred and ninety million years after the beginning, and in 2025 a team confirmed another, MoM z fourteen, at slightly earlier times still. These galaxies are surprisingly bright and, in some cases, surprisingly large, and Webb has found many more bright galaxies in the first five hundred million years than most models predicted. Explaining why, whether star formation was more efficient, the stars were brighter or more massive than today's, or some galaxies had growing black holes adding light, is one of the liveliest debates in astronomy.

The black holes are even more puzzling. Quasars, galaxies whose cores outshine all their stars because gas is pouring into a giant black hole, have been found less than seven hundred million years after the beginning, powered by black holes of more than a billion times the mass of the Sun. How did black holes grow so large so quickly? A black hole formed by the death of a first-generation star might have weighed a hundred Suns. To reach a billion Suns in a few hundred million years, it would need to swallow gas almost continuously at the maximum possible rate, which seems unlikely. One alternative is direct collapse: in special conditions, a giant cloud of gas might collapse straight into a black hole of tens of thousands of solar masses, giving it a head start. In 2023, X-ray observations by the Chandra telescope, combined with Webb, found a black hole in a galaxy called UHZ one, about four hundred and seventy million years after the beginning, whose properties seemed to fit this heavy-seed idea. Webb has also found a surprising population of compact red objects, nicknamed little red dots, that may be hidden growing black holes, wrapped in dense gas.

Meanwhile the first stars and their successors had changed the chemistry of the universe. Each generation of massive stars exploded, spreading carbon, oxygen, iron and other elements. Dust formed. By a billion years, some galaxies already had considerable amounts of heavy elements and dust; the ALMA telescope in Chile has detected carbon, oxygen and dust in galaxies from this period through their radio and millimetre glow. The ingredients of planets, and of life, were being assembled.

And what of our own galaxy? The oldest stars of the Milky Way formed during this era. Some of the globular clusters orbiting it, dense balls of hundreds of thousands of ancient stars, are more than twelve billion years old. Astronomers studying the motions and chemistry of stars, with the European Gaia satellite, have begun to trace the Milky Way's own early history, including the small galaxies it swallowed. The very first stars that went into our galaxy formed in the first billion years.

From here, cosmic history becomes the history of galaxies: the peak of star formation about ten billion years ago, the slow settling of spirals, the formation of the Sun and Earth about four and a half billion years ago, and the takeover of dark energy, which began to accelerate the expansion about five billion years ago. That is another story. But everything in it rests on the foundations laid in the first billion years. When you look at the night sky, the hydrogen in every star was made in the first three minutes, the pattern of the galaxies was set by quantum jitters during inflation, and the heavy elements in your body were forged in stars descended from those first beacons of cosmic dawn.
